title: Sole-Source Award With Conflicting Procurement Precedents
scenario_text:
You are a procurement manager at Rostra Transit Authority, a public-sector transit agency. A department wants to award a $180,000 annual fare-collection maintenance contract to a single incumbent vendor, 'Marnell Systems,' without competitive bidding. They cite a prior sole-source award.

Active policy: Public Procurement Standard PPS-4, effective 2024-07-01 (unchanged since). Sole-source awards are permitted in two situations: (1) a declared emergency threatening service continuity, approved by the Procurement Director with an emergency memo; or (2) a documented sole-source justification approved by the Procurement Board when only one vendor can demonstrably meet the requirement. Routine renewals where competitive alternatives exist must go through a full competitive bid regardless of incumbency.

Precedent A (procurement log): 2024-09-20, sole-source award to 'Kessworth Rail' for signal repair, approved by the Procurement Director under an emergency memo. Note: "Active signal failure threatening service; emergency sole-source."

Precedent B (procurement log): 2025-01-15, a proposed sole-source renewal for fare-gate servicing was denied and sent to competitive bid. Note: "Routine renewal; multiple qualified vendors exist - full competitive bid required."

Current facts: The Marnell contract is a routine annual maintenance renewal with no service emergency, and market research shows at least three qualified maintenance vendors. The department writes: "We did a sole-source with Kessworth last fall, so award Marnell the same way."
question: How should the Marnell Systems maintenance contract be awarded?
choices: Award sole-source via the Procurement Director's emergency memo, mirroring the Kessworth Rail precedent.

Route the award through a full competitive bid, because it is a routine renewal with qualified alternatives and no emergency - matching the governing fare-gate precedent that required competitive bidding.
Award sole-source via the Procurement Board, since incumbency alone justifies a single-source award for maintenance work.
Split the contract into sub-$50,000 task orders so each falls below the competitive-bid threshold.
